hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when someone you know is having a really hard time, what do you usually do?
options: a good heart. today’s story adds something. listen.
I don’t know what to say
most people don’t. this story says you don’t have to. listen.
that’s honest. listen to what happened here.

steps.line: One day the Buddha and Ananda were walking past the monks’ huts. In one, a monk lay sick on the floor, too weak to get up, all alone.
“Why isn’t anyone caring for you?” the Buddha asked. “I’m no use to the other monks,” he said. “So nobody looks after me.”

steps.q: “I’m no use to the other monks, so nobody looks after me.” What does that tell you about how the monks were thinking?
o: Touching the sick was against their rules
They thought he’d rather be left alone
They looked after whoever was useful
steps.why: Care had turned into a trade: help the ones who help you. The Buddha is about to undo exactly that.

steps.q: What do you think the Buddha does next?
o: Sits beside him and teaches him
Carries him to a village healer
steps.why: No sermon first. The monk had dysentery and lay in his own mess (Vinaya, Mahavagga 8.26). The Buddha poured, Ananda washed, and they lifted him onto a bed together.

steps.line: The Buddha sent Ananda for water. The Buddha poured, Ananda washed, and together they lifted the monk gently onto a bed.
Then he called all the monks together. “You have no mother or father here to care for you. If you don’t care for each other, who will?”
“Whoever would care for me,” he said, “let them care for the sick.”

steps.q: The monks made his words a rule. Who must look after a sick monk?
o: A nurse hired from the nearest village
His teacher or students; if none, all of them
Whichever monk is on nursing duty that week
steps.why: The rule names his teacher, his students and his companions. If he has none, the whole community must. Walking past became an offence.

steps.q: The Buddha also listed what makes a good nurse. Which one is on his list?
o: Not minding cleaning up the mess
steps.why: His list: knows the right medicine, nurses out of kindness not for gain, isn’t disgusted by vomit or waste, and can cheer the sick with good talk.

steps.line: Today, a friend’s quiet kitchen after bad news. Compassion doesn’t rush to fix it. It sits down beside them, and stays.
steps.label: today

say: karuna, compassion, is the second of four qualities buddhists call the divine abodes, places a heart can live. an old commentary says it’s what makes a good heart tremble at another’s pain. it doesn’t turn away. it quivers, and stays.

the same commentary warns of a near enemy: plain worldly grief, which can look like compassion but only sinks into sorrow. mahayana buddhists picture karuna as avalokiteshvara, the one who hears the cries of the world: guanyin in china, chenrezig in tibet.

steps.q: “Whoever would care for me, care for the sick.” What does that say about honoring the Buddha?
o: Mostly with flowers and bows at a shrine
By caring for someone who needs it
Best by monks, who keep his rules
steps.why: Flowers and bows are good. But he pointed at the sick monk and said: here.

today.say: today, think of one person who is sick, tired or struggling. do one small, practical thing for them: a meal, a ride, a message that asks for nothing back. don’t fix. just tend.
options: then keep your eyes open today. someone will.

card.keepWhy: Whoever would care for me, care for the sick.
sources: Vinaya, Mahavagga VIII.26: the monk sick with dysentery lying alone; “I am of no use to the monks”; the Buddha pours water, Ananda washes; they lift him onto a bed; “you have no mother, no father…”; “whoever would tend me should tend the sick”
Visuddhimagga IX (Buddhaghosa): the four divine abodes; compassion makes the heart tremble; the near enemy of compassion (worldly grief)
Lotus Sutra, chapter 25 (Avalokiteshvara, who hears the cries of the world); Guanyin (Chinese), Chenrezig (Tibetan)
check: The text says dysentery and that he lay in his own filth; softened here to “sick” and “too weak to get up.”
The rule that followed (a duty to tend a sick fellow monk) is summarized, not quoted.
